title: The best calcium sources without dairy

seo.title: Best calcium sources without dairy
seo.meta_description: Calcium-set tofu, sardines with bones, fortified plant milk, tahini, and leafy greens can provide calcium without dairy. Absorption varies by food.
seo.search_intent: Find strong non-dairy calcium sources and compare serving amounts and absorption.

excerpt: You can meet calcium needs without dairy, but the source matters. One cup of fortified soy milk often provides about 300 mg, 5.3 oz calcium-set tofu can provide 300–500 mg or more, and 3.5 oz sardines with bones roughly 350–380 mg. Greens such as kale and bok choy provide less per serving but their calcium is relatively well absorbed.
content_html:
A dairy-free diet does not have to be low in calcium, but non-dairy sources differ both in total calcium and in how much the body can absorb. Tofu and plant milks also vary enough that the label can change the answer completely.

Practical sources by serving

FoodServingCalcium
Fortified soy milk1 cup~300 mg
Calcium-set tofu5.3 oz / 150 g~300–500+ mg
Canned sardines with bones3.5 oz / 100 g~350–380 mg
Tahini2 tbsp / 30 g~120–200 mg
Cooked kale~5 oz / 150 g~200 mg
Cooked bok choy~5 oz / 150 g~140–160 mg

Tofu and fortified beverages vary widely, so the specific product label is the best reference.

Tofu can be excellent or modest

Tofu made with calcium sulfate can contain a large amount of calcium. Products made primarily with magnesium chloride or nigari may contain much less. Two firm tofu blocks can therefore look similar and have very different calcium numbers.

Sardines are high because the bones are eaten

The small bones soften during canning and become edible. That mineralized tissue explains why sardines with bones contain far more calcium than boneless fish fillets.

Greens differ in absorption

Kale and bok choy contain calcium with relatively good bioavailability. Spinach has plenty of total calcium on paper but also contains high oxalate levels, which bind calcium and sharply reduce absorption.

That is why a milligram-only ranking can be misleading.

Fortified plant milk can approach dairy milk

Many soy, oat, and almond beverages are fortified to around 300 mg per cup. Added calcium can settle, so shaking the carton before pouring helps distribute it evenly.

Nuts and seeds add calcium but come in small portions

Sesame, tahini, and almonds contribute calcium, but their usual serving sizes are modest and calorie-dense. They are useful contributors rather than always being the easiest way to obtain several hundred milligrams at once.

The useful takeaway

Calcium-set tofu, fortified plant beverages, and sardines with bones are among the easiest ways to get several hundred milligrams in one serving. Greens, tahini, almonds, and legumes can fill in the rest.

faq.question: What non-dairy food is highest in calcium?
faq.answer: Calcium-set tofu, sardines with bones, and fortified plant milks can each provide several hundred milligrams per serving.

faq.question: Is spinach a good calcium source?
faq.answer: It contains calcium, but oxalates greatly reduce absorption. Kale and bok choy generally provide more bioavailable calcium.

faq.question: Does all plant milk contain calcium?
faq.answer: No. Many products are fortified, but some are not. Check the label and shake fortified beverages before pouring.
